claim: Lpar1-EGFP subplate neurons comprise two morphological subtypes: fusiform SPNs with local axons and pyramidal SPNs with axons that extend through the marginal zone.
source: These SPNs comprise of two morphological subtypes: fusiform SPNs with local axons and pyramidal SPNs with axons that extend through the marginal zone.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by morphological reconstructions shown in Figure 2.

claim: Fusiform Lpar1-EGFP SPNs receive translaminar synaptic input up until the emergence of whisker barrels.
source: The former receive translaminar synaptic input up until the emergence of the whisker barrels, a timepoint coincident with significant cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by LSPS mapping data in Figure 3.

claim: The emergence of whisker barrels coincides with significant cell death in the subplate.
source: The former receive translaminar synaptic input up until the emergence of the whisker barrels, a timepoint coincident with significant cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry and TUNEL staining data in Figure 4.

claim: Pyramidal Lpar1-EGFP SPNs receive local input from the subplate at early ages.
source: In contrast, pyramidal SPNs receive local input from the subplate at early ages but then – during the later time window – acquire input from overlying cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by LSPS data in Figure 3.

claim: Pyramidal Lpar1-EGFP SPNs acquire input from overlying cortex during the later time window (P5-8).
source: In contrast, pyramidal SPNs receive local input from the subplate at early ages but then – during the later time window – acquire input from overlying cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by LSPS data in Figure 3.

claim: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs receive sparse thalamic innervation throughout early postnatal life.
source: Combined electrical and optogenetic activation of thalamic afferents identified that Lpar1-EGFP SPNs receive sparse thalamic innervation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by combined electrical and optogenetic stimulation experiments in Figure 7.

claim: Only 11% of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs exhibit responses to both electrical and optogenetic stimulation of thalamic afferents.
source: However, only two cells (11% of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs), with properties consistent with type 1 EPSCs, exhibited responses to both 470 nm light and electrical stimulation; no EGFP+ cells showed synaptic responses to light alone.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 7i.

claim: Subplate neurons are thought to play a role in nascent sensory processing in neocortex.
source: Subplate neurons (SPNs) are thought to play a role in nascent sensory processing in neocortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: The canonical role of SPNs is to support the establishment of thalamocortical synapses onto L4 neurons.
source: The canonical role of SPNs is to support the establishment of thalamocortical synapses onto L4 neurons (Kanold and Luhmann, 2010; Kanold et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies have reported that SPNs receive thalamocortical input prior to innervation of L4 neurons.
source: In support of this model, previous studies have reported that SPNs receive thalamocortical input prior to innervation of L4 neurons (Kanold et al., 2003; Friauf and Shatz, 1991; Zhao et al., 2009; Molnár et al., 2003; Higashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: SPNs are proposed to form feed-forward connections onto thalamo-recipient L4 neurons in a transient circuit.
source: In turn, SPNs are proposed to form feed-forward connections onto thalamo-recipient L4 neurons in a transient circuit that is eliminated upon establishment of the mature thalamocortical connectivity in L4 (Viswanathan et al., 2012; Hanganu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A large proportion of SPNs undergo programmed cell death during the first postnatal week in the mouse cortex.
source: While a large proportion of SPNs undergo programmed cell death during the first postnatal week in the mouse cortex (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013), the surviving SPNs form a thin, compact structure below L6, termed L6b in mature neocortex (Marx et al., 2017; Zolnik et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Surviving SPNs form a thin, compact structure below L6, termed L6b in mature neocortex.
source: While a large proportion of SPNs undergo programmed cell death during the first postnatal week in the mouse cortex (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013), the surviving SPNs form a thin, compact structure below L6, termed L6b in mature neocortex (Marx et al., 2017; Zolnik et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs form a layer of two to three cells deep adjacent to the white matter tract in neonatal S1BF.
source: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs form a layer of two to three cells deep adjacent to the white matter tract in neonatal S1BF (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the image in Figure 1a.

claim: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs have an intrinsic electrophysiological profile consistent with regular firing pyramidal cells.
source: We established that SPNs had an intrinsic electrophysiological profile consistent with regular firing pyramidal cells (Figure 1b,c) by injecting both depolarising and hyperpolarising current steps (500 ms) of increasing amplitude into cells recorded at resting membrane potential in current clamp configuration.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiological traces in Figure 1b,c.

claim: There is a progressive maturation of intrinsic properties of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs across P1-8.
source: Analysis of passive (Figure 1d–f) and active (Figure 1g–i) properties revealed a progressive maturation of intrinsic properties across the ages tested broadly in line with previous reports (Hanganu et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1d-i, with citation to previous literature.

claim: Input resistance (RIN) of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs decreases significantly over development from P1-8.
source: Specifically, we observed a statistically significant decrease in input resistance (RIN) (Figure 1e) and membrane time constant (Figure 1f), as well as increase in rheobase (Figure 1g), spike amplitude (Figure 1h), and maximum firing frequency (Figure 1i) over development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1e.

claim: Membrane time constant of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs decreases significantly over development from P1-8.
source: Specifically, we observed a statistically significant decrease in input resistance (RIN) (Figure 1e) and membrane time constant (Figure 1f), as well as increase in rheobase (Figure 1g), spike amplitude (Figure 1h), and maximum firing frequency (Figure 1i) over development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1f.

claim: Rheobase of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs increases significantly over development from P1-8.
source: Specifically, we observed a statistically significant decrease in input resistance (RIN) (Figure 1e) and membrane time constant (Figure 1f), as well as increase in rheobase (Figure 1g), spike amplitude (Figure 1h), and maximum firing frequency (Figure 1i) over development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1g.

claim: Spike amplitude of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs increases significantly over development from P1-8.
source: Specifically, we observed a statistically significant decrease in input resistance (RIN) (Figure 1e) and membrane time constant (Figure 1f), as well as increase in rheobase (Figure 1g), spike amplitude (Figure 1h), and maximum firing frequency (Figure 1i) over development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1h.

claim: Maximum firing frequency of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs increases significantly over development from P1-8.
source: Specifically, we observed a statistically significant decrease in input resistance (RIN) (Figure 1e) and membrane time constant (Figure 1f), as well as increase in rheobase (Figure 1g), spike amplitude (Figure 1h), and maximum firing frequency (Figure 1i) over development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1i.

claim: Pyramidal-like Lpar1-EGFP SPNs have a prominent apical dendrite projecting into L6a.
source: It was evident from our reconstruction of 19 of these cells that Lpar1-EGFP SPNs fell into two categories based on dendritic arbor and, specifically, the presence or absence of an apical dendrite (Figure 2a,b): (1) pyramidal-like SPNs with a prominent apical dendrite projecting into L6a and (2) fusiform SPNs that lacked an apical dendrite but instead exhibited bitufted dendrites that extended horizontally in the subplate and white matter tract.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by morphological reconstructions in Figure 2a,b.

claim: Fusiform Lpar1-EGFP SPNs lack an apical dendrite and exhibit bitufted dendrites that extend horizontally in the subplate and white matter tract.
source: It was evident from our reconstruction of 19 of these cells that Lpar1-EGFP SPNs fell into two categories based on dendritic arbor and, specifically, the presence or absence of an apical dendrite (Figure 2a,b): (1) pyramidal-like SPNs with a prominent apical dendrite projecting into L6a and (2) fusiform SPNs that lacked an apical dendrite but instead exhibited bitufted dendrites that extended horizontally in the subplate and white matter tract.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by morphological reconstructions in Figure 2a,b.

claim: The axon of pyramidal Lpar1-EGFP SPNs ascends through the overlying cortex, with the majority projecting to the marginal zone/L1.
source: Overlaying the axonal arbor of reconstructed morphologies revealed a further difference between these two populations: the axon of pyramidal SPNs (Figure 2d) ascended through the overlying cortex, with majority of cells projecting to the marginal zone/L1 (n = 9/12 cells, with the remaining three axons severed in L2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by axonal reconstructions in Figure 2d.

claim: The axon of fusiform Lpar1-EGFP SPNs is largely restricted to the SP with a few collaterals extending into L6a.
source: In contrast, the axon of fusiform cells was largely restricted to the SP with a few collaterals extending into L6a (Figure 2e) and no axon projecting to more superficial layers (n = 7/7 cells).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by axonal reconstructions in Figure 2e.

claim: The proportion of fusiform Lpar1-EGFP SPNs decreases from P5 onward.
source: Morphologies were recovered across all recorded ages; however, the proportion of fusiform cells decreased from P5 onward (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2f.

claim: All EGFP+ cells in the SP at P3 are GABA-negative.
source: This confirmed that EGFP+ cells in the SP were all GABA-negative (0/79 Lpar1-EGFP SPNs co-expressed GABA), while the vast majority (84%; 16/19) of EGFP+ profiles in L5 were GABA+, consistent with our previous characterisation of the SP (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013) and L5b interneuron populations (Marques-Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2g.

claim: 84% of EGFP+ profiles in L5 at P3 are GABA+.
source: This confirmed that EGFP+ cells in the SP were all GABA-negative (0/79 Lpar1-EGFP SPNs co-expressed GABA), while the vast majority (84%; 16/19) of EGFP+ profiles in L5 were GABA+, consistent with our previous characterisation of the SP (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013) and L5b interneuron populations (Marques-Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 2g.

claim: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs are glutamatergic projection neurons.
source: These data identify Lpar1-EGFP SPNs as glutamatergic projection neurons that fall into two subtypes based on their morphology: (1) fusiform cells that innervate the SP and (2) pyramidal cells whose axons extend through the entire depth of the developing cortex to ramify extensively through the margin zone/L1 (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GABA immunohistochemistry showing no co-expression with EGFP in SP.

claim: From the earliest time points recorded (P1-2), Lpar1-EGFP SPNs receive distinct columnar glutamatergic input.
source: From the earliest time points recorded (P1–2) SPNs received distinct columnar glutamatergic input, either from SP and adjacent cortex (L6a) alone, or from both SP/L6a and more superficial cortex; patterns of innervation that we termed 'local' and 'translaminar' respectively (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS mapping data in Figure 3b.

claim: At P1-2, Lpar1-EGFP SPNs exhibit two patterns of glutamatergic innervation: 'local' from SP/L6a alone, or 'translaminar' from both SP/L6a and more superficial cortex.
source: From the earliest time points recorded (P1–2) SPNs received distinct columnar glutamatergic input, either from SP and adjacent cortex (L6a) alone, or from both SP/L6a and more superficial cortex; patterns of innervation that we termed 'local' and 'translaminar' respectively (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS mapping data in Figure 3b.

claim: Translaminar Lpar1-EGFP SPNs at P1-2 receive input from the cortical plate that is absent in local SPNs.
source: The average laminar profile of local (n = 15) and translaminar (n = 8) SPNs at P1–2 revealed that the latter received input from the cortical plate (CP) absent in local SPNs (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS data in Figure 3c.

claim: At P3-4, translaminar input onto Lpar1-EGFP SPNs becomes more prominent with the source primarily focused in the lower CP, presumptive L4.
source: This translaminar input became more prominent over the next two postnatal days (P3–4; Figure 3d) with the source primarily focused in the lower CP, presumptive L4.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS data in Figure 3d.

claim: At P5-6, the majority (84%) of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs are dominated by local SP/L6a input.
source: In contrast, at P5–6, we recorded relatively few translaminar neurons with the majority (84%) dominated by local SP/L6a input.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS data in Figure 3e.

claim: All Lpar1-EGFP SPNs that received translaminar input from P1 to P4 were of the fusiform subtype.
source: Recovered morphologies of SPNs mapped from P1 to P4 (n = 15) revealed that all the SPNs, which received translaminar input, were of the fusiform subtype (n = 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined LSPS and morphological data.

claim: Of the 12 SPN morphologies recovered from P5 to P8, 9 cells received local glutamatergic input and were all of the pyramidal subtype with one exception.
source: Of the 12 SPN morphologies recovered from P5 to P8, 9 cells received local glutamatergic input. These were all of the pyramidal subtype with the exception of the only fusiform morphology recovered from ourLSPS experiments during this later window.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined LSPS and morphological data.

claim: Transient fusiform Lpar1-EGFP SPNs are the primary recipients of early translaminar input from the cortical plate up until P4.
source: Taken together these data suggest that transient fusiform SPNs are the primary recipients of early translaminar input from the cortical plate (Figure 3i), up until P4 when they become less apparent in our sample.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined LSPS and morphological data.

claim: Pyramidal Lpar1-EGFP SPNs are dominated by local glutamatergic input from SP/L6a at early ages.
source: In parallel, pyramidal SPNs are dominated by local glutamatergic input from SP/L6a at early ages (Figure 3i), but acquire varied translaminar input from more superficial layers from P5 onward.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS data.

claim: At P5-6, there is a significant increase in TUNEL+ profiles compared to P3-4.
source: This revealed a similar pattern of programmed cell death to our Casp-3 experiments, in that TUNEL+ cells were primarily located in the white matter at P3–4 (Figure 4e). However, at P5–6, we observed a significant increase in TUNEL+ profiles (Figure 4f) that included Lpar1-EGFP SPNs (Figure 4f,g).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by TUNEL staining data in Figure 4f,g.

claim: The increase in cell death at P5-6 is not restricted to the subplate but occurs across the white matter, subplate, and adjacent infragranular layers.
source: Moreover, it was evident that this increase was not restricted to the subplate (Figure 4f), so we further quantified the density of TUNEL+ profiles across the white matter, subplate, and adjacent infragranular layers at both time points, analysis that identified a surge in cell death at this later time point across the cortical layers sampled (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantification in Figure 4h.

claim: A small proportion of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs undergo cell death at the transition between P4 and P5.
source: Overall, this suggests that while a small proportion of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs undergo cell death at the transition between P4 and P5, this is not specific to subplate and likely represents a wider reconfiguration of the circuit at the transition to columnar signalling in S1BF at this time (Dupont et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by TUNEL and Caspase-3 data in Figure 4, with citation to previous literature.

claim: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs receive either local or translaminar GABAergic input across both P1-4 and P5-8 time windows.
source: Similar to our previous assessment of glutamatergic input, it was evident that SPNs received either local (Figure 5c,f) or translaminar input (Figure 5d,g) across both time windows.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS mapping data in Figure 5.

claim: Prior to P5, Lpar1-EGFP SPNs with translaminar GABAergic input receive prominent columnar input from L5.
source: Prior to P5, SPNs with local (Figure 5c) and translaminar (Figure 5d) input were evident in similar numbers with the latter receiving prominent columnar input from L5 (Figure 5b,d,e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS mapping data in Figure 5b,d,e.

claim: From P5 onward, the majority (11/16) of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs receive primarily local GABAergic synaptic input.
source: From P5 onward, we observed primarily local GABAergic synaptic input onto SPNs (n = 11/16)(Figure 5f), with the source of translaminar GABAergic input highly variable in location resulting in a diffuse average input profile (Figure 5g) with a more-or-less even distribution across the depth of cortex (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS mapping data in Figure 5f.

claim: Translaminar GABAergic input onto Lpar1-EGFP SPNs prior to P5 is highly focused within the immediate column.
source: Indeed, translaminar GABAergic input onto SPNs prior to the emergence of whisker barrels at ~P5 was highly focused within the immediate column (Figure 5i).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by columnar analysis in Figure 5i.

claim: Four out of seven recovered morphologies from P1-4 GABAergic mapping experiments were fusiform cells that received translaminar input.
source: Recordings in the early time window yielded seven morphologies, of which four were fusiform cells that received translaminar input; the remaining three recovered neurons were the pyramidal subtype, of which two received local input (Figure 5k).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined LSPS and morphological data.

claim: SST+ interneurons form a key component of early postnatal translaminar circuits.
source: Somatostatin (SST+) interneurons form a key component of early postnatal translaminar circuits (Marques-Smith et al., 2016; Anastasiades et al., 2016) and have been shown to drive synapse formation and circuit maturation (Oh et al., 2016; Tuncdemir et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is an increase in SST+ interneuron IPSC amplitude onto Lpar1-EGFP SPNs at P5-6 compared to P3-4.
source: We observed an increase in IPSC amplitude across all light powers tested greater or equal to minimal stimulation in the P5–6 when compared to the P3–4 time window (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by optogenetic stimulation data in Figure 6a.

claim: The increase in SST+ interneuron IPSC amplitude at P5-6 results from an increase in innervation rather than an increase in quantal size.
source: However, we observed no difference in the amplitude of IPSCs recorded in Sr-ACSF between P3–4 and P5–6 time windows (Figure 6d) despite the significant difference in amplitude under control conditions (Figure 6b,c). This suggests the observed increase in amplitude at this time point results from an increase in innervation by SST+ INs rather than an increase in quantal size.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Sr-ACSF experiments in Figure 6b-d.

claim: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs receive two distinct input profiles from SST+ interneurons at P1-4: local SP/L6a versus translaminar infragranular input.
source: Our analysis revealed two distinct input profiles for SPNs at this time (Figure 6e,f): local SP/L6a versus translaminar infragranular SST+ interneuron input.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LSPS uncaging of ATP data in Figure 6e,f.

claim: Local input SPNs from SST+ interneurons were pyramidal cells (3/3 recovered morphologies).
source: Similar to our previous findings with both glutamatergic and global GABAergic input, local input SPNs were pyramidal cells (3/3 recovered morphologies), whereas SPNs that received translaminar synaptic input were predominantly fusiform (2/3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined LSPS and morphological data.

claim: SPNs that received translaminar synaptic input from SST+ interneurons were predominantly fusiform (2/3).
source: Similar to our previous findings with both glutamatergic and global GABAergic input, local input SPNs were pyramidal cells (3/3 recovered morphologies), whereas SPNs that received translaminar synaptic input were predominantly fusiform (2/3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined LSPS and morphological data.

claim: GABAergic input onto Lpar1-EGFP SPNs from infragranular SST+ interneurons precedes the reciprocal connection between SST+ cells and L4 spiny stellate neurons during the L4 CPP (P4-9).
source: The presence of GABAergic input onto SPNs from infragranular SST+ interneurons precedes our previously reported reciprocal connection between these SST+ cells and L4 spiny stellate neurons during the L4 CPP (P4–9) (Marques-Smith et al., 2016) and then onto L2/3 pyramidal cells during the emergence of L4 to L2/3 feed-forward connections (Anastasiades et al., 2016; Bureau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Infragranular SST+ interneurons sequentially innervate thalamo-recipient layers through early postnatal life in S1BF.
source: Taken together, this evidence suggests that infragranular SST+ interneurons sequentially innervate thalamo-recipient layers through early postnatal life in S1BF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the temporal sequence of SST+ interneuron connectivity.

claim: Electrical stimulation evoked EPSCs in 76% of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs recorded across P1-8.
source: Electrical stimulation evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in the majority (76%) of SPNs recorded across the time window studied, although there was a drop in incidence between the P1–4 and P5–8 (chi-square test X2 (1, N = 56) = 5.364, p = 0.021) time windows (Figure 7b);
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrical stimulation data in Figure 7b.

claim: There is a drop in incidence of electrically evoked EPSCs in Lpar1-EGFP SPNs between P1-4 and P5-8 time windows.
source: Electrical stimulation evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in the majority (76%) of SPNs recorded across the time window studied, although there was a drop in incidence between the P1–4 and P5–8 (chi-square test X2 (1, N = 56) = 5.364, p = 0.021) time windows (Figure 7b);
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 7b.

claim: Electrically evoked EPSCs in Lpar1-EGFP SPNs can be divided into two populations based on 10-90% rise time and amplitude: type 1 (large amplitude, low jitter) and type 2 (small amplitude, high jitter).
source: All EPSCs with a latency > 10 ms and/or jitter > 1.0 ms (Figure 7d) were then excluded from our analysis leaving 32 SPNs that could be further divided into two populations based on 10–90% rise time and amplitude (Figure 7e): type 1 (n=9), large amplitude (55.3 pA ± SD 14.3), low jitter (0.20 ms ± SD 0.07), versus type 2 (n=23), small amplitude (14.9 mV ± SD 5.8), high jitter (0.41 ms ± SD 0.17) EPSCs (Figure 7f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by analysis of electrical stimulation data in Figure 7e,f.

claim: Thalamic connectivity to Lpar1-EGFP SPNs could be as low as 17% if type 1 EPSCs represent true orthodromic TC-EPSCs.
source: However, thalamic connectivity could be as low as 17% if type 1 EPSCs recorded in SPNs represent true orthodromic TC-EPSCs, considerably lower than connectivity reported in previous studies of SP in early postnatal ages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the proportion of type 1 EPSCs.

claim: Blue light reliably evokes inward currents in thalamic relay neurons following Olig3 Cre conditional expression of ChR2.
source: To validate our optogenetic strategy at early postnatal ages, we first recorded from thalamic relay neurons in Lpar1-EGFP;Olig3 Cre;Ai32 mice and established that we could evoke (1) reliable inward currents in whole-cell patch-clamp mode in response to blue, 470 nm light (Figure 7h, top panel), and (2) time-locked action potentials in cell-attached mode (Figure 7h, bottom panel) from the earliest time points recorded (P1) (n=5 VB cells).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by optogenetic validation data in Figure 7h.

claim: Only 2 out of 19 Lpar1-EGFP SPNs (11%) exhibited responses to both electrical and optogenetic stimulation of thalamic afferents.
source: Across the whole time window tested (P1–8), we obtained recordings under both stimulation protocols in 19 EGFP+ cells. Of these, nine cells across all ages tested (P1–8) had short latency, low jitter (<1 ms) EPSCs in response to electrical stimulation (types 1 and 2) (Figure 7i). However, only two cells (11% of Lpar1-EGFP SPNs), with properties consistent with type 1 EPSCs, exhibited responses to both 470 nm light and electrical stimulation; no EGFP+ cells showed synaptic responses to light alone.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined electrical and optogenetic stimulation data in Figure 7i.

claim: Only 3 of 15 (27%) non-EGFP+ SPNs receive thalamic input as identified by combined electrical and optogenetic stimulation in the P1-4 time window.
source: To establish whether sparse thalamocortical connectivity is a property of the Lpar1-EGFP subtypes alone, we then recorded from non-EGFP+ SPNs. Using our combined electrical and optogenetic stimulation strategy, we identified thalamic input onto only 3 of 15 (27%) non-EGFP+ SPNs in the P1–4 time window.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined electrical and optogenetic stimulation data.

claim: The majority of EPSCs observed after electrical stimulation (type 2) arise from antidromic activation of cortico-thalamic projection neurons.
source: We therefore believe that the majority of EPSCs observed after electrical stimulation, termed type two here, arise from antidromic activation of cortico-thalamic projection neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the lack of optogenetic responses in cells with type 2 EPSCs.

claim: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs in S1BF receive both thalamic and cortico-thalamic input in the first postnatal week, but thalamic input is relatively sparse.
source: Taken together these data suggest that Lpar1-EGFP SPNs in S1BF receive both thalamic and cortico-thalamic input in the first postnatal week, but that the former is relatively sparse, contacting only a small subset of the total population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by combined electrical and optogenetic stimulation data.

claim: Lpar1-EGFP SPNs do not adhere to the canonical role reported for SPNs in primary sensory cortex.
source: Our study identifies that Lpar1-EGFP SPNs in S1BF have an additional novel function that does not conform to the canonical model for SPNs established across sensory cortices, wherein SPNs act as relay cells for thalamic input to L4 (Kanold and Luhmann, 2010; Tolner et al., 2012; Allendoerfer and Shatz, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by the sparse thalamic connectivity data.

claim: Fusiform Lpar1-EGFP SPNs are ideally placed to interpret and amplify sparse thalamic input alongside emergent signalling from the cortical plate.
source: We propose that fusiform Lpar1-EGFP SPNs are ideally placed to interpret and amplify sparse thalamic input alongside emergent signalling from the cortical plate, thereby providing a template – through their innervation of other SPNs including the Lpar1-EGFP pyramidal subtype – for the columnar circuit assembly up until the emergence of whisker barrels in L4 at ~P4–P5.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a proposed model based on the data presented.

claim: Prenatal spontaneous thalamic activity plays an instrumental role in determining the columnar organization of S1BF.
source: It is evident that prenatal spontaneous thalamic activity plays an instrumental role in determining the columnar organization of S1BF (Antón-Bolaños et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Shortly before birth, thalamic afferent fibres are restricted to the subplate and thalamic stimulation elicits activity that spreads laterally through this and immediate adjacent infragranular layers.
source: Shortly before birth thalamic afferent fibres are restricted to the subplate and thalamic stimulation elicits activity that spreads laterally through this and immediate adjacent infragranular layers (Higashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Lpar1 (Edg2) is one of a number of markers that delineate SPN diversity.
source: Lpar1 (Edg2) is one of a number of markers previously shown to delineate SPN diversity (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013), with the cohort labeled by this line one of the earliest born subtypes with peak neurogenesis at embryonic day (E)11.5.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The cohort labeled by the Lpar1-EGFP line is one of the earliest born SPN subtypes with peak neurogenesis at embryonic day (E)11.5.
source: Lpar1 (Edg2) is one of a number of markers previously shown to delineate SPN diversity (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013), with the cohort labeled by this line one of the earliest born subtypes with peak neurogenesis at embryonic day (E)11.5.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EGFP expression in Lpar1-EGFP SPNs is evident at embryonic ages.
source: EGFP expression is evident in this population at embryonic ages (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013), increasing to label both SP and non-SP neurons by the end of the first postnatal week (Marques-Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The temporal dynamics of connections in S1BF are quite different from those reported for A1, notably the early afferent input from L4.
source: However, the temporal dynamics of the connections that we observe in S1BF, notably the early afferent input from L4, are quite different to those reported for A1 wherein L4 input emerges in the second postnatal week (Viswanathan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by comparison with cited literature.

claim: The disparity in timing of L4 input between S1BF and A1 could underpin differences in the role of SP in circuit maturation between sensory areas.
source: This disparity in timing could underpin differences in the role of SP in circuit maturation between sensory areas and suggests that the cytoarchitecture of sensory areas differs from the outset.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the observed differences.

claim: Pyramidal Lpar1-EGFP SPNs are likely conduits for thalamic activity, recruiting pyramidal cells and GABAergic interneurons in more superficial cortex via their L1 axon collaterals.
source: Our data suggest that Lpar1-EGFP pyramidal SPNs are likely conduits for such activity, recruiting pyramidal cells and GABAergic interneurons in more superficial cortex (Friauf and Shatz, 1991; Che et al., 2018) via their L1 axon collaterals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the morphological and connectivity data, with citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurons in the superficial cortical layers provide feedback columnar glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic input onto transient fusiform SPNs.
source: In turn, neurons in the superficial cortical layers provide feedback columnar glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic input onto transient fusiform SPNs thus completing the circuit (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by LSPS mapping data.

claim: The sparse nature of thalamic engagement with the subplate coupled with an indirect relay mechanism represents a plausible substrate to ensure the emergence of spatially distinct columnar circuits in S1BF.
source: This indirect mechanism could provide the necessary framework for the interpretation of early thalamic signals resulting in columnar organisation. Indeed, such a mechanism coupled with the sparse nature of thalamic engagement with the subplate represents a plausible substrate to ensure the emergence of spatially distinct columnar circuits in S1BF.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculative model based on the data.

claim: The relay of thalamic input via L1 moves away from a L4-centric view of early thalamic engagement.
source: Moreover, relay of thalamic input via L1 moves away from a L4-centric view of early thalamic engagement, more in line with distributed thalamocortical input across all six layers of neocortex (Feldmeyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data, with citation to previous literature.

claim: The subplate is a transient layer in the developing neocortex located between the emergent cortical plate and the underlying white matter.
source: The subplate is a transient layer in the developing neocortex located between the emergent cortical plate and the underlying white matter (Kostovic and Rakic, 1990; Hoerder-Suabedissen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The subplate contains a diverse population of neuronal subtypes that differ in terms of molecular markers, morphology, neurotransmitter identity, and connectivity.
source: It contains a diverse population of neuronal subtypes that differ in term of molecular markers (Hoerder-Suabedissen and Molnár, 2013), morphology (Marx and Feldmeyer, 2013), neurotransmitter identity (Boon et al., 2019), and connectivity (Viswanathan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPNs are relatively mature when compared to cortical neurons in the more superficial cortical plate early in development.
source: Electrophysiological studies performed in primary sensory areas suggest that SPNs are relatively mature when compared to cortical neurons in the more superficial cortical plate early in development (Marx and Feldmeyer, 2013; Luhmann et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPNs are regarded as key mediators of early spontaneous and sensory-evoked activity.
source: As such they are regarded as key mediators of early spontaneous and sensory-evoked activity (Tolner et al., 2012) and direct circuit maturation (Kanold and Luhmann, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPNs promote the maturation of cortical GABAergic neurons.
source: In parallel, SPNs also promote the maturation of cortical GABAergic neurons (Kanold and Shatz, 2006), pioneer cortico-thalamic projections (McConnell et al., 1989), secrete proteins that control extracellular matrix composition, attract and guide thalamocortical fibres, regulate plasticity and myelination (Kondo et al., 2015), and control the radial migration of cortical neurons at embryonic ages (Ohtaka-Maruyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPNs pioneer cortico-thalamic projections.
source: In parallel, SPNs also promote the maturation of cortical GABAergic neurons (Kanold and Shatz, 2006), pioneer cortico-thalamic projections (McConnell et al., 1989), secrete proteins that control extracellular matrix composition, attract and guide thalamocortical fibres, regulate plasticity and myelination (Kondo et al., 2015), and control the radial migration of cortical neurons at embryonic ages (Ohtaka-Maruyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPNs secrete proteins that control extracellular matrix composition, attract and guide thalamocortical fibres, regulate plasticity and myelination.
source: In parallel, SPNs also promote the maturation of cortical GABAergic neurons (Kanold and Shatz, 2006), pioneer cortico-thalamic projections (McConnell et al., 1989), secrete proteins that control extracellular matrix composition, attract and guide thalamocortical fibres, regulate plasticity and myelination (Kondo et al., 2015), and control the radial migration of cortical neurons at embryonic ages (Ohtaka-Maruyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SPNs control the radial migration of cortical neurons at embryonic ages.
source: In parallel, SPNs also promote the maturation of cortical GABAergic neurons (Kanold and Shatz, 2006), pioneer cortico-thalamic projections (McConnell et al., 1989), secrete proteins that control extracellular matrix composition, attract and guide thalamocortical fibres, regulate plasticity and myelination (Kondo et al., 2015), and control the radial migration of cortical neurons at embryonic ages (Ohtaka-Maruyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies performed in A1 have identified two distinct physiological populations of SPN: those that receive feedback glutamatergic input from L4 and a second cohort that only receives local input.
source: While previous studies performed in A1 have identified two distinct physiological populations of SPN – those that receive feedback glutamatergic input from L4 and a second cohort that only receives local input (Viswanathan et al., 2012) – this has not been explicitly linked to SPN identity per se.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Thalamic input is a determinant of columnar organization in late embryonic somatosensory cortex.
source: Moreover, recent evidence suggests that while thalamic input is a determinant of columnar organization in late embryonic somatosensory cortex (Antón-Bolaños et al., 2019), such activity pre-dates the transition to the mature cytoarchitecture and columnar signalling unit (Dupont et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Thalamic activity pre-dates the transition to the mature cytoarchitecture and columnar signalling unit in somatosensory cortex.
source: Moreover, recent evidence suggests that while thalamic input is a determinant of columnar organization in late embryonic somatosensory cortex (Antón-Bolaños et al., 2019), such activity pre-dates the transition to the mature cytoarchitecture and columnar signalling unit (Dupont et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The P4-5 time point represents the switch from transient SP to layer 6b (L6b) in S1BF.
source: This diversification of synaptic input fits with the rapid transition to columnar signalling previously reported at P5 (Dupont et al., 2006) and suggests that this time point represents the switch from transient SP to layer 6b (L6b) (Zolnik et al., 2020) in S1BF.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the data, with citations to previous literature.
